summary: A 1970 note by M. Elie titled Getting rid of marking, about removing the marking field in the host-IMP interface. It is part of a discussion with RFC 67.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 64 proposes removing marking from messages because it adds bits and can require extra work at the receiver. The suggested interface change uses a counter to handle word boundaries instead.

subtitle: A proposed Host-IMP interface change to avoid marking bits.

tldr.problem: Marking lets a sending host align message text to its word boundary, but it adds bits and can require shifting at a receiving host with a different word length.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal adds a counter to the Host-IMP interface shift register so hardware can handle word boundaries without transmitting the marking bits.
tldr.outcome: The author presents the change for consideration and leaves the decision to others.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 64 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC presents a proposed change to the Host-IMP interface for consideration.

sections.title: Why Marking Costs Work
sections.content:
Marking was introduced so message text could start at a word boundary in the sending host. The note says this does not suit a receiving host with a different word length and adds bits that carry no useful message text.

In its example, the receiving host must detect the first 1 after the leader and shift the message before translating it into its internal code. The note estimates about 12 microseconds per double word for this work.
sections.plainLanguage: Marking helps the sender align a message, but a receiver with a different word size may need to shift the data. The extra marking and padding bits also take up space in transmission.

sections.title: Transmission Efficiency in the Examples
sections.content:
The note gives a one-character example in which 112 transmitted bits carry 8 bits of text, for an efficiency factor of 0.07. It says suppressing marking would raise this to 0.10.

For a 32-bit text, the note estimates an increase from 0.28 to 0.4. For one-packet messages, it says the increase would still be 3%.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show how marking and padding can add many transmitted bits around a small amount of text. The note estimates higher efficiency if marking is removed.

sections.title: Counter-Based Interface Change
sections.content:
For host-to-IMP traffic, the proposal adds a counter that starts at the beginning of a message and increments for each bit. At 32 bits, it signals that a word is complete, requests another word for the shift register and resets; unused bits in the last leader word are not transmitted.

For IMP-to-host traffic, the counter also counts to 32. The interface lets the shift register fill to the host's word boundary without taking more bits from the IMP, so the next text bit starts the next word.
sections.plainLanguage: The interface counts bits and signals when it has a full word. The receiving side uses the count to align the next text bit without relying on marking in the message.

sections.title: A Suggested Modification
sections.content: The author says the combined cost of sending marking bits and reshaping received text makes the modification worth considering. The note describes it as a suggestion and says the decision is outside the author's competence.
sections.plainLanguage: The author asks others to consider the interface change. The note does not claim that the change was adopted.
